column6: The commentary reads 87:2's creating and proportioning bodily; Genesis narrates God forming the first human from ground and breathing life into him, adding the dust-to-living-body sequence.
Job addresses God as the maker who fashioned and made him, a personal bodily counterpart to the commentary's account of creation and arrangement.
Job pictures his own formation in the womb as milk becoming cheese; this gives concrete gestational process to the commentary's fetal-forming life-stage reading.
Job says God clothed and knit these body parts together, closely specifying the bodily ordering that the commentary hears in 87:2–3.
The psalmist credits God with forming inward parts and knitting him in his mother's womb, making explicit the prenatal bodily scene behind the commentary's life-stage reading.
The psalm's hidden, intricately woven formation in the body's depths adds a concealed-making image to the commentary's womb and shaping sequence.
The psalm joins an embryo not yet formed to days written beforehand; it brings prenatal formation together with the measured lifespan heard in the commentary's qaḍara and life-cycle reading.

column5: formed in womb before prophetic commission
column6: Jeremiah is known and set apart before being formed in the womb; this shares the commentary's divine prenatal formation while adding vocation before birth.
Solomon presents himself as mortal and descended from the first human formed from earth; this places the commentary's bodily ordering within a Jewish reflection on universal human origin.
Solomon describes being molded in flesh in his mother's womb over ten months, a direct gestational counterpart to the commentary's fetal formation.
Solomon says he was swaddled and cared for, giving a concrete childhood instance of the commentary's branch of Rabb as raising a child.

column5: from leaving the womb to returning to the mother of all living
column6: Sirach describes human toil as spanning birth from the womb to return to earth, an unusually explicit lifespan parallel to the commentary's womb-to-aging sequence.

column5: all things ordered by measure, number, and weight
column6: Wisdom says God ordered all things by measure, number, and weight; this closely specifies the commentary's reading of 87:3 as putting each thing in its particular measure and form.
God says he has borne and carried Israel from the womb; this makes the commentary's Rabb-as-raising image a lifelong divine-care metaphor, though Isaiah speaks collectively of Israel.
The same oracle promises to carry Israel into old age and gray hairs, bringing the commentary's womb-to-senescence life arc under one image of divine care.

column5: God relied on from the womb
column6: The speaker says God has been his hope from birth and benefactor from the womb, an individual prayer counterpart to the commentary's nurturing life-cycle sense of Rabb.
The psalmist asks not to be abandoned in old age; this makes the commentary's senescence sense concrete as a prayer about divine care at life's late stage.

column5: fruitful and green in old age
column6: The righteous remain fruitful, fresh, and green in old age; the verse uniquely joins the commentary's aging body with its surah's pasture and vegetation imagery.

column5: remember the Creator before aging days
column6: Ecclesiastes urges remembrance of the Creator before difficult years and old age arrive, joining the commentary's Creator-centered bodily life course to its age-related reading.
The poem pictures trembling hands, bent strength, failing teeth, and dim eyes; it gives physical detail to the commentary's otherwise brief old-age sense.
Isaiah identifies all flesh with grass and its glory with a field flower; this makes the commentary's pairing of human body and drying pasture an explicit image of mortality.

Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flowers with God's enduring word; beside the surah's dried pasture and its enduring-afterlife contrast, it adds a biblical word-versus-mortal-life formulation.

column5: human days like grass and field flower
column6: The psalm compares human days and flourishing to grass and a flower, directly joining bodily lifespan to vegetation as the commentary does in its life-stage and pasture reading.
The flower disappears when wind passes; this adds the disappearance of mortal life to the commentary's warning carried by drying pasture.

column5: fetus taught Torah, then made to forget
column6: The Talmud says an angel teaches the fetus Torah in the womb and strikes it at birth so it forgets; this meets the commentary's womb association for the root of 87:6 with that verse's recitation and not-forgetting, while the Talmud's fetus and Qur'anic addressee differ.

column5: living soul rendered as speaking spirit
column6: Onqelos interprets the formed human's life-breath as a speaking spirit; this Jewish reading connects the bodily formation discussed for 87:2 with the surah's adjacent gift of recitation in 87:6.
Luke describes Jesus growing as a child, becoming strong and filled with wisdom; it supplies a concrete growth-to-maturity scene for the commentary's Rabb-as-child-rearing branch.

column5: Jesus advances in age and stature
column6: Jesus increases in wisdom, stature, and favor; this is a direct bodily-growth counterpart to the commentary's reading of maturation through a human life.

column5: seed must die to be made alive
column6: Paul's seed analogy makes death the condition for new life; beside the commentary's embryo-to-resurrection argument and its formed-body/drying-plant pairing, it joins plant and bodily renewal.

column5: God gives each seed its body as willed
column6: Paul says God gives each seed its own body as he wills, a close specific counterpart to the commentary's measured and specially formed body under 87:3.
Paul's contrast between a perishable body sown and an imperishable body raised directly answers the commentary's link between bodily creation and resurrection.
Paul distinguishes the body sown as natural from the body raised as spiritual, extending the commentary's formed body and resurrection connection into a claim about transformation.
Paul pictures all creation groaning in labor pains; this brings the commentary's womb-centered bodily life cycle into a cosmic creation image.
Believers groan while awaiting bodily redemption; this connects the commentary's formed human body and resurrection argument with Paul's future transformation of the body.

column5: new birth through imperishable seed and word
column6: Peter says his readers have been born anew through imperishable seed by God's living word; this meets the commentary's womb-and-recitation cluster and introduces a Christian new-birth image.
Peter quotes Isaiah that all flesh and its glory are like grass and flower; this directly joins the commentary's mortal body and withering pasture.
Peter contrasts withering flesh with the Lord's enduring word, applied to the proclaimed gospel; it develops the commentary's pasture and lasting-life contrast through Christian proclamation.
John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will abides forever; this closely matches the surah's worldly-life versus better, enduring hereafter contrast.
Jesus contrasts earthly treasure vulnerable to decay with treasure secured in heaven; this gives a concrete image to the surah's preference for worldly life over what is better and enduring.
Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal, giving a Christian formulation of the surah's worldly-life and enduring-afterlife contrast.
The infant receives breath and cries at birth; it extends the commentary's prenatal-to-lifespan sequence across the body's emergence from the womb.
Even a king's birth has no different beginning; this Jewish reflection makes the commentary's bodily life stages universal rather than a lexical claim about one person.
All people share one way into life and one way out; it frames the commentary's womb-to-old-age arc with mortality and a common human course.

column5: fear of heights and journey to the eternal home
column6: The old-age poem moves from bodily frailty to the human going to an eternal home, adding the life's endpoint to the commentary's aging stage.

At death, dust returns to earth and spirit to God; this reverses the dust-and-breath formation of Genesis 2:7 and supplies an endpoint to the commentary's bodily lifespan, without itself arguing for resurrection.
The psalm assigns human life seventy or, at strength, eighty years, then says it passes swiftly; this makes the commentary's measured-body and old-age senses an explicit lifespan measure.
Proverbs contrasts young men's strength with gray hair as elders' splendor, giving a compact scriptural life-stage pair beside the commentary's maturity and senescence readings.

The earth yields first a stalk, then an ear, then full grain; this plant-growth sequence meets the commentary's child-raised-in-stages and pasture imagery while remaining an agrarian, not human, account.
The ripe crop is harvested, completing Mark's growth sequence; beside the commentary's vegetation growth and drying, it adds the endpoint of maturity and harvest.

column5: birth brings a child into the world and ends remembered anguish
column6: Jesus compares the disciples' sorrow to labor pain that gives way to joy when a child is born into the world; this meets the commentary's delivery-nearness sense for al-dunya and its womb-related reading of qaraʾ, without claiming either Arabic branch as the verse's literal meaning.
Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and lose one's life; this states explicitly the danger implicit in the commentary's identification of preferring worldly life.

The Syriac Peshitta uses the cognate q-r-ʾ verb when Jesus stands to read Isaiah; this is a specific scriptural reading use beside 87:6's recitation, while the commentary's separate womb-related branch should not be transferred to this verse.

column5: newborn with cord uncut, unwashed, and unswaddled
column6: The commentary's camel idiom mentions fetal membranes not gathered; Ezekiel's allegory depicts a newborn left with its cord uncut and without birth care. The objects differ, but both make perinatal handling concrete.

column5: bones formed in a pregnant woman's womb
column6: Ecclesiastes contrasts the unknown formation of bones in the womb with God's work as maker of all; this directly joins the commentary's fetal body-shaping and divine ordering, while stressing that the process is hidden.

column5: one maker fashioned both people in the womb
column6: Job grounds equality between himself and his servant in the same maker forming them in the womb; this adds an ethical consequence to the commentary's account of shared human bodily formation.

column5: taught Ephraim to walk and lifted him by the arms
column6: God recalls teaching Israel as a child to walk and carrying him; this is a concrete child-rearing scene for the commentary's Rabb-as-raising-a-child sense.

column5: lifted infant and bent down to feed
column6: God describes lifting Israel like an infant and bending down to feed him; this extends the commentary's nurturing life-stage image into hands-on parental care.

column5: Creator says he formed Israel from the womb
column6: Isaiah joins forming the addressee in the womb to the Lord's making of all things; this ties the commentary's prenatal formation directly to universal creation.

column5: Sarah and Abraham advanced in age; her monthly cycle had ceased
column6: The narrative names the aged body's reproductive limit before Isaac's promised birth, bringing the commentary's old-age and approaching-birth stages together in one concrete case.

column5: Sarah conceives and bears Isaac in old age
column6: Isaac is born to Sarah at the time God promised, when Abraham is old; this gives a narrative reversal in which the commentary's late-life stage becomes the setting for birth.

column5: Sarah nurses a son in Abraham's old age
column6: Sarah marvels that she has borne and nursed a son in Abraham's old age; this uniquely combines the commentary's child-rearing and senescence stages.
Job says a person's days are determined, months numbered, and limit set; this closely meets the commentary's reading of 87:3 as assigning each thing its measure, here applied to human lifespan.

column5: sinews, flesh, skin, and breath restore a body
column6: In a vision interpreted as Israel's restoration (37:11), God reassembles the dry bones with bodily tissues and breath; this supplies a detailed scriptural image of the ordered body and renewed life discussed in the commentary.

column5: body assembled but still without breath
column6: The bones have sinews, flesh, and skin, yet no breath; this makes bodily formation and animation distinct stages, sharpening the commentary's creation-and-order sequence.

column5: breath summoned from the four winds to the slain
column6: The prophet is told to call breath into the slain so they may live; this joins the commentary's formed body with divine breath and revival, in a vision whose stated referent is exiled Israel.

column5: the breath enters and the slain live
column6: The bodies stand alive after the breath enters them; this is a vivid resurrection-like image beside the commentary's argument from bodily formation to God's power to raise the dead, though Ezekiel interprets the vision corporately.

column5: dead awaken and earth gives birth to shades
column6: Isaiah calls the dead to live and the earth to give birth to its dead; this joins bodily resurrection to birth imagery, meeting the commentary's fetal formation and resurrection argument.

column5: sleepers in dust awake to opposed destinies
column6: Daniel says many sleeping in the dust awake to everlasting life or shame; this gives a Hebrew Bible resurrection counterpart to the commentary's creation-to-resurrection argument and places judgment after bodily renewal.

Rabbi Meir answers a question about resurrection by pointing to grain buried bare that emerges clothed; this Jewish argument uses plant transformation to make renewed embodiment imaginable, meeting the commentary's pairing of bodily creation, resurrection, and vegetation.
The angel says Elizabeth, called barren, is now six months pregnant in her old age; this precisely brings the commentary's old-age and approaching-birth senses into one Christian narrative.

column5: first Adam living soul, last Adam life-giving spirit
column6: Paul interprets Genesis 2:7 by contrasting the first Adam as living soul with the last Adam as life-giving spirit; this links the commentary's formed human and breathed life to resurrection through a Christian reading of Adam.

column5: Gehenna's worm does not die and fire is not quenched
column6: Jesus uses Isaiah's undying-worm and unquenched-fire image as a warning about Gehenna; beside the surah's great fire and its continuation that the condemned neither die nor live, it gives a Christian judgment image with a different formulation.

After the human is taken from the ground, God says he will return to it; this completes the earth-to-body sequence cited in the commentary with its bodily endpoint before the Qur'anic resurrection argument.

column5: martyr expects to receive his limbs again
column6: A tortured brother says he received his limbs from heaven and hopes to receive them again; this Jewish witness makes resurrection bodily and specific, beside the commentary's inference from bodily creation to raising the dead.

column5: king has no resurrection to life
column6: The youngest brother expects God to raise him to life, while the king has no resurrection to life; this adds the commentary's bodily revival theme together with opposed postmortem destinies.

Paul says Christ will transform the body of humiliation to conform to his glorious body; this is a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's ordered body and resurrection, with transformation rather than mere return.

column5: Israel forgets the God who gave it birth
column6: Moses accuses Israel of forgetting the God who gave it birth; this meets the commentary's womb and child-raising senses beside 87:6's promise not to forget, but reverses the roles: Israel forgets its divine parent.
Isaiah asks whether a mother can forget the son of her womb, then says God will not forget Zion; this meets the commentary's womb, nurture, and not-forgetting cluster through a maternal-memory image.

column5: human born of woman, brief as a fading flower
column6: Job joins birth from a woman to a short life that flowers and withers; this connects the commentary's lifespan arc to its body-and-drying-vegetation warning.

column5: Job asks whether a dead person will live again
column6: Job asks whether a human who dies will live again and says he would wait for release; this places the commentary's confident move from bodily formation to resurrection beside a Hebrew lament that frames renewed life as a question and hope.

column5: time to be born and time to die
column6: Ecclesiastes frames human life with a time for birth and a time for death, a concise lifespan formula beside the commentary's womb-to-old-age reading.

column5: measure of days and life's end
column6: The psalm asks God to make known the measure of its days and its end; this makes the commentary's measured-life reading of 87:3 a prayer about human limits.
The psalm asks God to teach people to number their days; it joins the commentary's measured lifespan to the guidance of 87:3, with numbering leading to wise living.
At Mary's greeting, the infant leaps in Elizabeth's womb; this adds a concrete action of the fetus within the womb to the commentary's prenatal life-stage imagery.

column5: Sarah conceives beyond the age for childbearing
column6: Hebrews interprets Sarah's conception as faith in the promise despite her age; beside the commentary's old-age and birth stages, it adds a Christian reading of the Genesis reversal.

column5: childhood put away on becoming an adult
column6: Paul contrasts speaking and thinking as a child with becoming an adult; this gives the commentary's child-to-maturity sequence a distinct ethical and interpretive use.

column5: milk-fed child unskilled in the word
column6: Hebrews likens the inexperienced hearer to an infant needing milk; this meets the commentary's child-rearing and maturation image while applying it to learning, not bodily formation.
Hebrews contrasts infants with mature people whose faculties are trained; this develops the commentary's growth-to-maturity sequence as discernment acquired over time.

column5: no one can add a cubit to stature or lifespan
column6: Jesus asks whether anxiety can add a cubit to a person's ἡλικία, read as stature or lifespan; this specific ambiguity meets the commentary's measured body and measured human course.

column5: field grass clothed today, burned tomorrow
column6: Jesus says God clothes grass that is thrown into the oven the next day; the image joins the commentary's pasture that withers to bodily care and fire, while Matthew's point is trust rather than judgment.

column5: people seek death, but death flees
column6: During the locust torment, people desire death without finding it; this concretely meets the surah's adjacent statement that those in the fire neither die nor live, although Revelation's torment scene is not itself the final lake of fire.

column5: resurrected people can no longer die
column6: In Jesus' reply about the resurrection, those deemed worthy of that age can no longer die; this gives a Christian contrast to the surah's condemned who neither die nor live.

Isaiah's closing vision has worshipers view the corpses of rebels with undying worms and unquenched fire; beside 87:12–13, it shares fire and undying imagery but depicts corpses rather than living people unable to die.
